## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.71013.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.71013.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Acceptance summary:

Kaplan and colleagues build upon their earlier work using genetic phenotypes to find and analyze mutations that determine how mRNA start sites are chosen. Here they provide convincing genetic evidence supporting the model that TFIIH pushes downstream DNA back into the RNA polymerase active site, creating a window within which the polymerase can choose particular start sites. This will primarily interest those in the transcription field thinking about initiation mechanisms.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Ssl2/TFIIH Function in Transcription Start Site Scanning by RNA Polymerase II in Saccharomyces cerevisiae" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Kevin Struhl as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) Provide a more general description of TSS-seq to account for a broad readership and re-analyze data using altered cutoff filters to determine the impact of those filters on the observed variability of transcriptional shifts.

2) Deposit processed data into GEO to enable easier re-use by the scientific community.

3) Improve overall readability of the manuscript. There was a unified sense of too much density by all of the reviewers to the point that impact could be reduced. The authors are encouraged to stream line text and figures throughout the entire paper to make messaging more clear.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall, the strength of this study is readily apparent and that is derived from the level of detail the authors had in their analysis to make it is thorough as possible. I commend the authors on their efforts. However, this same strength is also the primary weakness of the paper. The presentation is so dense that it is an exhausting study to get through. The density is apparent at all levels including the number of figures, figure panels, and the writing in general. The study would have much higher impact if it was more streamlined. While it is not my habit to display editorial activism as a reviewer, I feel this paper would benefit from improved presentation. Along these same lines, as a general comment, the authors could significantly improve the messaging of this paper by including short conclusion/wrap-up sentences for each subsection to inform the reader of the overall importance of the data. As it stands now, most sections abruptly end with the description of the last panel so a reader is left trying to determine the take-home point. I provide a list of additional suggestions for the authors to consider to make the overall narrative more digestible for a general readership.

1) Figure 1: The authors do not introduce what 'lys2-128 Spt-' phenotype actually is. They are reliant on their previous work but there is not enough description as to what the molecular basis of this is so one cannot ascertain its importance. The authors could consider removing it altogether as none of the mutants appeared to display this phenotype.

2) Figure 1: The authors should consider moving panel E to the supplement. I understand its value as a positive control, but the general concept of 'start site shifting' is straightforward and their actual data are clear. By removing it, the individual panels of the figure can be larger.

3) Figure 1: I am having trouble understanding the quantitative basis for the author's conclusion that ssl1 mutants (DEAD and 508) are different than the Pol II mutant (E1103G). Comparing bins 2 and 5, for the E1103G the change relative to wild-type is ~0.25 and ~-0.25 respectively. Whereas the DEAD is ~0.12 and ~-0.15 and 508 is ~0.12 and ~-0.1. These seem really similar. Can the authors provide some statistical evidence that this is the trend or just dampen their claim?

4) Figure 1: I am not sure what the XPB mutants add to the story. The authors should add rationale as to why these mutants are important to analyze and how the results fit into the greater narrative.

5) Figure 2: the authors introduce Spt- phenotypes as 'transcriptional related' phenotype but this is not clear what this phenotype is. It appears to be related to His+, but the authors introduce it without a reasonable explanation. This is especially critical because the authors are contrasting the lack of overlap between Spt- and MPAs phenotypes in the ssl mutants.

6) Figure 3A is a well-constructed schematic but it would be helpful to match the color-coding in panels 3C/D in order to understand three-dimensionally where the mutant phenotypes reside. The authors do point some of this out in the text but it is hard to ascertain this looking at the figure.

7) Figure 4: the choice of coloring could be improved. It is very difficult to see differences, particularly in Figure 4B.

8) I would recommend either shifting the positions of Figures 8 and 9 or moving 9 to the supplement. I also feel that the model presented in Figure 8 is difficult to follow as there is only limited reference to it in the results. The authors could consider featuring a model as the focus of their opening paragraph of the discussion. This would nicely tie together all aspects of the study.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. I would recommend expanding the description of the TSS-Seq analysis. In particular, I would recommend expanding on the filters that the authors might have applied to select the gene TSS to investigate. Depending on the sequencing depth and read threshold used, the variability for the shift or with of the investigated TSS could change dramatically. I do not think that will alter dramatically their results but will enable its reanalysis.

2. I would also encourage to add the numeric data associated to the different heatmap show in the manuscript (i.e., Figure 4 and 5). That will facilitate the reuse of the authors data by the scientific community.

3. In the same line, I would encourage the authors to deposit in GEO the processed TSS files (e.g., BedGraph, BigWig or similar). Currently in SRA only the raw data are available, and significant work is needed to make them reusable. Providing browsable filed with IGV as is standard for all GEO deposits will further increase the impact of the author's work.

results.result: TSS selection in S. cerevisiae occurs by a unidirectional scanning mechanism where the PIC assembles at an upstream core promoter and initiates at positions ~40-120 bp downstream.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C13, and C14 establish the scanning mechanism as prior knowledge supported by extensive citations. This forms the foundational model upon which the current study builds, and is well-established in the field.

results.result: Ssl2/XPB, a subunit of TFIIH, drives promoter scanning through ATP-dependent DNA translocase activity, as demonstrated by single-molecule studies showing DNA compaction and bubble formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C15-C19 describe prior work establishing Ssl2/TFIIH's role in scanning through biochemical and biophysical studies. Multiple independent lines of evidence from optical and magnetic tweezer experiments support this mechanism.

results.result: Existing ssl2 alleles show distinct transcription phenotypes: ssl2-DEAD and ssl2-508 exhibit MPAS and upstream TSS shifts by reducing downstream TSS usage, SSL2-1 shows His+ phenotype with downstream shifts, while ssl2-rtt and rad25-ts24 show no TSS effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C38 are directly supported by phenotyping data (Figure 1C) and primer extension analysis (Figure 1E). The quantitative distinction between ssl2 and Pol II alleles (C36) is demonstrated by comparing TSS usage patterns.

results.result: Human disease-related XPB mutations show varied effects in yeast: Q592* is lethal, T176P has no phenotype, while F156S and Y750* confer MPAS phenotypes and upstream TSS shifts. RED motif substitutions are lethal.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by viability assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and primer extension data (Figures 1F-G). The observation that some human disease alleles function in yeast (C44) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: Novel ssl2 alleles identified through genetic screening fall into two major classes: MPAS alleles (upstream shifting) with mutations distributed across the protein in conserved domains, and His+ alleles (downstream shifting) clustered N-terminally in the Tfb2-homologous domain. Spt- phenotype is found exclusively in His+ mutants, distinct from Pol II mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C45-C48, and C50 are supported by genetic screening data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2), structural mapping (Figure 2A-D), and sequence conservation analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). The distinct phenotypic patterns between ssl2 and Pol II mutants are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: TSS-shifting ssl2 substitutions map to functionally important regions including DNA-proximal surface residues and the Ssl2 N-terminal domain. Multiple substitutions at N230 produce opposite effects: N230D/S cause upstream shifts while N230I causes downstream shifts.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C57 are supported by structural mapping (Figure 2B-D) and TSS analysis data. The N230 position is particularly notable as different substitutions produce opposite phenotypes, suggesting a critical regulatory role.

results.result: ssl2 alleles alter TSS distributions differently from Pol II alleles: ssl2 MPAS alleles truncate downstream TSS usage rather than activating upstream sites as Pol II GOF alleles do, suggesting distinct mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 are supported by comparative primer extension analysis (Figure 2E-H). The distinct patterns of TSS shifts between ssl2 and rpb1 alleles are clearly demonstrated, supporting the inference of different mechanisms (C63).

results.result: TSS-seq analysis reveals that ssl2 alleles shift TSS distributions genome-wide, with mutant classes distinguished by hierarchical clustering that separates ssl2 and Pol II alleles.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by TSS-seq correlation analysis (Figure 3B-C) and hierarchical clustering (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). The genome-wide effects validate that single-promoter observations are predictive of global behavior.

results.result: ssl2 MPAS alleles shift median TSS positions upstream at most promoters by decreasing downstream signal, while His+ alleles shift positions downstream by increasing downstream usage. The magnitude of shifts correlates with phenotype strength but is less than for Pol II mutants. PCA distinguishes four major mutant classes.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 are comprehensively supported by TSS-seq heatmaps (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), median TSS shift analysis (Figure 4D-E), hierarchical clustering (Figure 4D), and PCA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B). Statistical significance is demonstrated (p < 0.0001).

results.result: ssl2 upstream shifting mutants narrow TSS spreads while downstream shifting mutants widen TSS spreads at the majority of promoters, demonstrating quantitatively and qualitatively distinct effects from Pol II mutants despite similar genetic phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by TSS spread analysis (Figure 5B-D), heatmaps (Figure 5C), and statistical comparisons showing significant differences from WT (p < 0.05). The distinction from Pol II mutants is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that ssl2 alleles narrowing TSS spreads are defective in scanning processivity due to decreased Ssl2/TFIIH translocase activity, while alleles widening spreads behave as processivity GOF alleles due to increased activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are explicitly stated as hypotheses to explain observed data. While the TSS spread changes are well-documented, direct biochemical evidence for altered processivity is not provided. This remains a model requiring biochemical validation.

results.result: Genetic interactions between ssl2 and Pol II alleles show primarily epistatic effects, contrasting with the additive/suppressive interactions between Pol II and TFIIB/TFIIF. Notably, there is near-complete absence of synthetic lethality between ssl2 and Pol II downstream shifting alleles.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by extensive genetic interaction data (Figure 6A-K, Figure 6—figure supplement 3). The epistatic patterns are clearly demonstrated and contrast with prior observations for other GTFs, supporting distinct functional roles.

results.result: Lethal interactions occur between ssl2 alleles and sua7-1 or tfg2Δ146-180 when single mutants shift TSS distributions in the same direction. When shifts are in opposite directions, complex epistatic interactions are observed with double mutants resembling tfg2Δ146-180 single mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 are supported by genetic interaction data (Figure 7A) and primer extension analysis (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The pattern of interactions suggests additional complexity beyond simple efficiency effects.

results.result: sub1Δ shows primarily additive interactions with ssl2 alleles at ADH1, with most upstream shifting ssl2 alleles showing mutual suppression of TSS shifts. Allele-specific interactions reveal sub1Δ is epistatic to ssl2 Y750* and ssl2 F498L shows unexpected synthetic lethality with both sua7-1 and sub1Δ.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 are supported by genetic interaction data (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and primer extension analysis (Figure 7D). The additive interactions and allele-specific exceptions are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Genetic interaction studies support a model of two distinct networks controlling TSS selection: one impinging on Pol II catalysis and initiation efficiency (Pol II, TFIIB, TFIIF), and another regulating TFIIH processivity (Ssl2, Sub1, potentially TFIIF).
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 integrate all genetic interaction data (Figure 8) into a coherent model. The epistatic patterns between networks and additive patterns within networks support this two-network model, though C96 includes supporting citations for TFIIB/TFIIF effects on Pol II activity.

results.result: ssl2 N230D and N230I shift PIC component localization (Sua7 and Ssl2) genome-wide with the same polarity as TSS shifts. ChIP-exo shifts are as strong or stronger than Pol II mutant shifts despite weaker TSS effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by ChIP-exo data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1). The observation that PIC shifts are stronger than TSS shifts suggests potential uncoupling between scanning and initiation, though this interpretation requires caution.

results.result: The study reveals that distinct classes of Ssl2 alleles in conserved residues alter initiation genome-wide through modulation of TFIIH processivity during promoter scanning. One class behaves as LOF, truncating scanning and narrowing TSS distributions, while another increases downstream usage and extends PIC localization, consistent with increased processivity. GOF alleles are dominant/codominant.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C105 summarize the study's major conclusions, integrating genomic data (TSS-seq, ChIP-exo), genetic data (dominance tests), and structural observations. While the processivity model (C102-C104) is well-supported by genetic and genomic evidence, direct biochemical demonstration of altered processivity is not provided.

results.result: Prior work established that mutations in Pol II, TFIIB, TFIIF, and Sub1 cause polar TSS shifts genome-wide. Hyperactive Pol II mutants shift TSSs upstream while hypoactive mutants shift downstream. Genetic interactions suggest these factors act in the same pathway during scanning, with TFIIB reducing and TFIIF increasing initiation efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C30 describe prior work by the authors and others, supported by extensive citations. These establish the context for the current study and the framework for interpreting ssl2 allele effects. The mechanistic interpretations (C24-C25, C29) are based on correlations between catalytic activity and TSS shifts.

results.result: The study proposes that ssl2 alleles alter TSS selection by modulating scanning processivity (not rate), and that promoter scanning outcome is determined by two networks: Pol II activity determining initiation efficiency within a scanning window, and Ssl2/TFIIH determining the width of the scanning window through processivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 represent the study's central model. C6 is directly supported by TSS spread data. C7's distinction between processivity and rate is supported by genetic interaction patterns showing epistasis rather than additivity. C8 integrates all findings into a coherent model, though direct biochemical evidence for processivity vs. rate distinction is not provided.
